answer.label: Written by (translated)
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine, well-known saying of Confucius — Analects, Book II, Chapter XVII — in the classic English translation by James Legge (1861). The Chinese original 知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也 is spoken by Confucius to his disciple Zhong You (Zi Lu), and Legge’s wording matches word for word.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Confucian Analects (Lunyu 論語), Book II, Chapter XVII
Confucius (551–479 BC), to his disciple Zhong You (Zi Lu)
知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也

source.excerpt: The Master said, ‘You, shall I teach you what knowledge is? When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it — this is knowledge.’
trail: The wording is James Legge’s, first printed in The Chinese Classics, Vol. 1 (1861), Confucian Analects, Book II, Ch. XVII, verse 9, as documented by Today in Science.
The Chinese Text Project ↗ shows the same passage (Wei Zheng 17) with Legge’s translation beside the original Chinese, confirming both the source and the translator.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the original 知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也 under the Analects, Book II, confirming the passage is authentic to Confucius.
source.excerptNote: Legge’s English, set beside the Chinese original 子曰：「由！誨女知之乎？知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也。」 at the Chinese Text Project.

sourceLink.text: Analects 2.17 (Wei Zheng) — Chinese original with Legge's translation, Chinese Text Project

source.rightsNote: The original Chinese Analects is ancient and long in the public domain. The exact English wording here is James Legge’s translation, first published in The Chinese Classics, Vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861) and revised in 1893 — both editions are well before 1931, so this translation is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: Confucius (Kong Qiu)
author.metaLine: 551–479 BC · Chinese philosopher, teacher & editor of the classics
author.bio: Confucius (Kong Qiu, courtesy name Zhongni) was a teacher and philosopher of the Spring and Autumn period whose sayings were gathered by later disciples into the Lunyu, or Analects. His ethics of learning, honesty, and self-cultivation shaped East Asian thought for two millennia. This line — that real knowledge means owning both what you know and what you don’t — is one of his most quoted teachings on intellectual honesty.

misattribution.heading: A real quote — but watch the paraphrases
misattribution.intro: This exact line is genuine Confucius. But Confucius is one of the internet’s biggest fake-quote magnets, and this teaching in particular circulates in loosened, translator-free paraphrases that people pass off as his literal words.

items.who: “Real knowledge is to know the extent of one’s ignorance.”
items.why: Widely shared as a direct Confucius quote, this is a loose modern rendering of the same passage (Analects 2.17), not a literal translation of the Chinese — it circulates with no translator or edition attached, as seen across sites like BrainyQuote ↗.

items.who: “To know what you know and what you do not know, that is true knowledge.”
items.why: A shortened restatement of Legge’s line that spreads without noting it is a paraphrase; the documented wording spoken to Zhong You is Legge’s fuller sentence quoted above.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought — and this specific wording — genuinely trace to Confucius via Analects 2.17 in James Legge’s 1861 translation; only the trimmed meme versions are unmoored paraphrases.

context.heading: Why it endured
lead: The saying compresses a whole theory of learning into one sentence: knowledge is not just what you have grasped, but the honesty to mark off what you have not. Confucius addresses it to his headstrong disciple Zhong You (Zi Lu), a warning against bluffing.

It has become a touchstone for intellectual humility, quoted alongside Socrates’ ‘I know that I know nothing’ as an ancient East-meets-West statement that admitting ignorance is itself a form of wisdom.
context.pull: To own what you know, and own what you don’t — that is knowledge.
